title: Chapter XXIII

teacherSummary.text: Victor pursues the creature across Europe to the Arctic, following taunting messages. His tale ended, Walton resumes writing: the ice traps the ship, the crew demands to turn south, and Walton yields. Victor dies. The creature appears over his body, mourns, condemns himself, and vows to die on a funeral pyre before vanishing into darkness.

vocabulary.definition: To go out of the way
vocabulary.context: I now related my history, briefly, but with firmness and precision, marking the dates with accuracy, and never deviating into invective or exclamation.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “deviate”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: She left me, and I continued some time walking up and down the passages of the house, and inspecting every corner that might afford a retreat to my adversary.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “inspect”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + spect (Latin specere, "to look"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: As I spoke, rage sparkled in my eyes; the magistrate was intimidated:—“You are mistaken,” said he, “I will exert myself; and if it is in my power to seize the monster, be assured that he shall suffer punishment proportionate to his crimes.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “intimidate”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The act of seizing, or the state of being seized
vocabulary.context: When I had concluded my narration, I said, “This is the being whom I accuse, and for whose seizure and punishment I call upon you to exert your whole power.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “seizure”: se- (Latin se-, "apart"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: I was possessed by a maddening rage when I thought of him, and desired and ardently prayed that I might have him within my grasp to wreak a great and signal revenge on his cursed head.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “madden”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: This address caused a considerable change in the physiognomy of my own auditor.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “auditor”: -or (Latin -or, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The show of an intention to inflict evil
vocabulary.context: But I discovered no trace of him, and was beginning to conjecture that some fortunate chance had intervened to prevent the execution of his menaces; when suddenly I heard a shrill and dreadful scream.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “menace”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: To feel a kind of thrilling sensation, as in hearing a shrill sound
vocabulary.context: As I heard it, the whole truth rushed into my mind, my arms dropped, the motion of every muscle and fibre was suspended; I could feel the blood trickling in my veins, and tingling in the extremities of my limbs.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “tingle”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: To come between, or to be between, persons or things
vocabulary.context: But I discovered no trace of him, and was beginning to conjecture that some fortunate chance had intervened to prevent the execution of his menaces; when suddenly I heard a shrill and dreadful scream.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “intervene”: inter- (Latin inter, "between") + ven (Latin venire, "to come"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: A violent stream, as of water, lava, or the like
vocabulary.context: There were no horses to be procured, and I must return by the lake; but the wind was unfavourable, and the rain fell in torrents.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “torrent”: -ent (Latin -ens, "one who, doing"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: The pursuit into the frozen north returns us to the frame setting.

significance: Creator and creation become mirror images, each driven solely by revenge.
discussionQuestions: How have Victor and the creature come to resemble each other?
Where does plot appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with nature versus nurture?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XXIII,” how does Shelley show loss and vengeance? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the plot you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XXIII develops the idea of loss and vengeance. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of plot and tone / mood shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses plot in Chapter XXIII to complicate the reader's understanding of loss and vengeance. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XXIII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of loss and vengeance responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XXIII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of loss and vengeance. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

options: To come between, or to be between, persons or things

satQuestions.passage: She left me, and I continued some time walking up and down the passages of the house, and inspecting every corner that might afford a retreat to my adversary. But I discovered no trace of him, and was beginning to conjecture that some fortunate chance had intervened to prevent the execution of his menaces; when suddenly I heard a shrill and dreadful scream. It came from the room into which Elizabeth had retired. As I heard it, the whole truth rushed into my mind, my arms dropped, the motion of every muscle and fibre was suspended; I could feel the blood trickling in my veins, and tingling in the extremities of my limbs. This state lasted but for an instant; the scream was repeated, and I rushed into the room.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter XXIII”?
options: The first death and growing guilt

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: How have Victor and the creature come to resemble each other? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are deviating, inspecting, intimidated, seizure, maddening. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “I now related my history, briefly, but with firmness and precision, marking the dates with accuracy, and never deviating into invective or exclamation.” Webster's says: To go out of the way. Now the word history: “deviate”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “inspect”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + spect (Latin specere, "to look"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “intimidate”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. The pursuit into the frozen north returns us to the frame setting. Why does this chapter matter? Creator and creation become mirror images, each driven solely by revenge. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for plot.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see plot, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to loss and vengeance.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Plot, Tone / mood, Characterization.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of plot. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XXIII,” how does Shelley show loss and vengeance? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the plot you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the costs of unchecked ambition? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
